items.title: [dagenslantbruk.se] Farmers and agribusinesses test AI to cut costs and improve crops
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Agricultural companies, researchers and farmers are using artificial intelligence for crop monitoring, breeding, irrigation and farm administration, as tools move from research into field trials. A survey previewed at the PLUSAGRI 2026 conference in Warsaw on Nov. 18 found that 53.9% of participating Polish farmers said they use AI; organizers planned to present findings on how farmers use the technology and how much they trust it. Sweden’s Lantmännen says it uses AI in plant breeding and to improve the use of fertilizer, crop protection products and water. Applications range from software that analyzes crop images and farm data to AI-guided irrigation. A European potato program supported by Cropin examined how farming practices affect water use and potato quality, while researchers have reported AI systems that identify crop models from agricultural data. A Chinese provincial study analyzed data from 2005 to 2023, while newer tools still require testing across crops and climates before broader use.

items.content_html:

Farmers and researchers are adapting to drought and extreme heat with soil checks, crop trials and changes to farm work. In Poland, soil scientist Bartłomiej Glina says growers should assess soil structure, compaction and water storage before relying on irrigation. Researchers in India screened linseed varieties for late-season heat tolerance, while Romanian teams tested sweet potatoes, peanuts and cowpea as alternative crops. Research on heat waves found that feedback between temperature, soil moisture and atmospheric pressure can increase the intensity of the most extreme events by 10%. In Senegal, workers report shorter hours in the fields as heat intensifies. In India’s Jarandi area, drought is threatening guava and sweet-lime orchards as wells and other water sources decline.

items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Farmers and researchers are testing soil, irrigation and crop-management measures as drought, flooding and extreme heat strain agriculture in Poland, Sweden and Senegal. At a Polish agriculture conference, experts said drought resilience depends on assessing soil conditions and improving long-term water retention. A Swedish research project is assessing a system designed to store water in dry periods and release it during floods. In Senegal, farmers and agricultural workers report hotter planting seasons and fewer hours in the fields, while shared irrigation along the Senegal River has become vital. The Swedish project will test the system under different climate scenarios and develop implementation guidance. Researchers say its effects on soil ecosystems and nutrient releases still need study.

items.title: [meatingplace.com] U.S. cattle placements hit October record low as supplies tighten
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

U.S. feedlots placed 1.891 million cattle in October, down 7% from a year earlier and the lowest October total in records dating to 1996, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported Nov. 20. The decline exceeded analysts’ expectations: placements were 92.7% of last year’s level, compared with an average forecast of 96.5%. Feedlots with capacity for at least 1,000 head held 11.59 million cattle on Nov. 1, down 1% year over year. October marketings fell 5% to 1.62 million head, the lowest October figure since records began. Hales Cattle Letter warned that continued heifer retention could further reduce marketings and slaughter, while packers face margin pressure in 2027.

items.title: [dagenslantbruk.se] Swedish farm profits improve, but investment plans remain cautious
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Swedish farmers report improved profitability and stronger confidence than in the spring, citing lower interest rates as a factor, but investment plans remain restrained. items.title: [stpetersburg.usf.edu] Study finds drought could cut cactus habitat by 80% by 2100
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

An international research team analyzed nearly 1,000 cactus species and found that more than a quarter could lose at least 80% of their suitable habitat by 2100 if severe droughts intensify. The researchers added drought projections to climate models, which commonly use long-term temperature and rainfall averages, and combined them with biodiversity records, field observations and community-science data. The projected losses could qualify affected species as Critically Endangered under criteria set by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), more than doubling the number of cacti in that category. Researchers say drought may also reduce growth or flowering without immediately killing plants, compounding threats from habitat destruction and illegal collection. The findings are expected to inform updated IUCN Red List assessments; the team says further research is needed to determine which life stages and biological processes drought affects.

items.title: [cyberscoop.com] Europol-led operation seizes malware infrastructure, finds 6.4 million stolen credentials
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Law enforcement agencies in nine countries, coordinated by Europol and Eurojust, disrupted infrastructure used by Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC, seizing 235 servers and 257 domains and identifying 6.4 million stolen credential records. German authorities said the records came from more than 40,000 victims. The malware services enabled credential theft, remote access and the delivery of ransomware; investigators also cleaned 681 websites compromised to spread Gootloader. Authorities plan to share victim data with notification services, including Have I Been Pwned. On Nov. 13, that service listed 179,745 email addresses linked to CastleRAT infections and 893,000 unique passwords observed more than 3 million times on infected computers. Police advised WordPress users to change credentials, enable multifactor authentication and patch vulnerabilities.
